title: Neora Valley National Park from Lava: seasons, permits and walks
summary: Neora Valley National Park, set up in 1986, is one of the least disturbed forests in the Eastern Himalaya and home to the red panda. Visit from Lava between mid-September and mid-June with a permit and a registered guide arranged at the Lava forest office. October–November and April–May are the best months.
meta_description: Neora Valley National Park guide: when it opens, permits and guides from Lava, what you can see, day walks, costs, where to stay and what to pack.

sections.heading: What Neora Valley is
paras: Neora Valley National Park lies in the east of Kalimpong district, where West Bengal meets Sikkim and Bhutan. It was declared a national park in 1986. The park rises from about 180 m near the plains to over 3,100 m at Rachela, its highest point on the Sikkim border. Within that range you pass from subtropical forest through broadleaf oak and laurel to rhododendron, bamboo and fir.

Much of the park has no roads and few trails, which is why it is one of the least disturbed forests in the region. It links with Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary in Sikkim and with forests in Bhutan, forming a larger wild corridor. The Neora river, which drains the valley, supplies water to Kalimpong town.
For visitors, the park is reached mainly from Lava on its northern side, with a lower entry from the Samsing side near the Dooars. This guide focuses on the Lava side, which most travellers use.

sections.heading: What you might see
paras: The park is best known for the red panda, which lives in the higher bamboo and oak forest. It is shy and rarely seen by day visitors; sightings mostly come from researchers, forest staff and people on longer treks. Other mammals recorded here include the Himalayan black bear, leopard, clouded leopard, goral, serow, barking deer and several small cats. Camera traps have also recorded tigers. You are unlikely to see most of these on a day walk.

Birds are the real reward. The park is listed as an Important Bird Area, and the forest between about 1,600 and 2,700 m holds laughingthrushes, barwings, fulvettas, sunbirds, woodpeckers, cuckoos, pigeons and raptors. The satyr tragopan, a pheasant with a crimson body and white spots, lives here and is a prize for birders. Spring brings breeding songs and colour.
The plants matter too: moss-covered oaks, tree ferns, many orchids and several rhododendron species that flower from March to May.

sections.heading: Seasons and closures
paras: The park is closed for the monsoon, normally from about 16 June to 15 September, in line with other national parks in North Bengal. It can also close at short notice for weather, fire risk or administrative reasons. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Permits, guides and fees
paras: You need an entry permit and a registered local guide to walk in the park. On the Lava side, both are arranged at the forest range office in Lava, usually early in the morning. Bring a photo ID for each person. Foreigners should carry their passports.

Fees change from time to time, so treat these as indicative for 2025–26. Expect an entry fee of roughly ₹100–200 per person, a guide fee of about ₹500–1,000 per group per day, and a vehicle fee if your car goes to the entry point. A car from Lava for the day costs about ₹1,500–2,500. Camera fees may apply for professional equipment.
Numbers can be limited on busy days, especially during the October holidays, so reach the office early or ask your lodge to help. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: How a day walk works
paras: After collecting the permit and guide, you drive from Lava to the park entry point and then walk. Day routes follow set trails through upper forest, usually 5–10 km in total, at a slow pace with frequent stops to look and listen. Most groups are back in Lava by mid-afternoon, before the mist and rain that often come later in the day.

The trails are uneven, with roots, rocks, mud and steep sections at over 2,000 m. Anyone who walks regularly will manage, but take it slowly. Longer treks deeper into the park, towards Rachela or down the valley, need special permission, porters and camping gear, and are best arranged through specialist operators.
If the park is closed or permits run out, good alternatives include Changey Falls near Kolakham, the forest roads around Lava for birding, and the trail between Lava and Rishop.
list: Start at the Lava forest office soon after it opens.
Walk quietly in small groups; noise scares off birds and animals.
Stay on the trail and with your guide at all times.
Carry all rubbish out of the park.
Do not feed animals, use bird-call playback or pick plants.

sections.heading: Where to stay and how to get there
paras: Lava is the base. The WBFDC nature resort, in forest just above the bazaar, is closest in spirit to the park, with cottages at about ₹1,500–3,500 a room, indicative. Homestays and small hotels in and around Lava cost about ₹1,200–2,000 a person with meals. Rishop, 11 km away at about 2,590 m, adds a great sunrise view, and Kolakham sits right on the park edge.

Lava is about 33 km from Kalimpong via Algarah, 1.5 hours by car, and about 105–110 km from Siliguri, 3.5–4 hours via Kalimpong or via Malbazar and Gorubathan. A few shared jeeps run from the Kalimpong motor stand to Lava, mostly in the morning. Plan two nights in Lava if the park walk is a priority, so you have a spare morning if weather or permits get in the way.

sections.heading: What to pack
paras: The forest is wet and cool even in the dry season, and temperatures at 2,000–2,700 m change quickly. Pack for rain and cold whatever the month.
list: Waterproof walking shoes or boots with good grip
A rain jacket and a warm fleece or down layer
Leech socks or gaiters from April to June and in late September
Binoculars and a field guide or birding app
Water, snacks and a packed lunch from your lodge
A small first-aid kit, sunscreen and insect repellent
Photo ID, cash for fees and a phone with offline maps

faqs.q: When is Neora Valley National Park open?
faqs.a: It is usually open from about mid-September to mid-June and closed for the monsoon from about 16 June to 15 September. The best months are October and November for clear weather, and April and May for birds and rhododendrons. Closures can happen at short notice. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get a Neora Valley permit?
faqs.a: On the Lava side, go to the forest range office in Lava early in the morning with photo ID for each person. Staff issue the entry permit and assign a registered guide. Your lodge or homestay can often help. Fees are paid locally and change from time to time, so carry cash.

faqs.q: How much does a Neora Valley visit cost?
faqs.a: Indicative 2025–26 costs: entry about ₹100–200 per person, a guide about ₹500–1,000 per group, and a car from Lava about ₹1,500–2,500 for the day, plus any vehicle or camera fees. A couple sharing a car and guide should budget roughly ₹3,000–4,000 for the day.

faqs.q: Is a guide compulsory in Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors must walk with a registered local guide. Guides know the trails, which split and are poorly marked, and they help spot birds and animals. They also make sure groups follow park rules and stay safe in thick forest where cloud can close in fast.

faqs.q: What are my chances of seeing a red panda?
faqs.a: Low on a day visit. Red pandas live in the higher, remote bamboo and oak forest and are shy and mostly active at dawn and dusk. Sightings are rare even for regular visitors. Go for the forest and the birds, and count a red panda as a stroke of luck.

faqs.q: Can I enter Neora Valley from Samsing?
faqs.a: Yes, there is a lower entry from the Samsing side, near the Dooars, with permits from the forest office there. It gives access to lower, warmer forest. Most travellers from Kalimpong use the Lava side. Rules for both entries can change. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Neora Valley suitable for children and older travellers?
faqs.a: Short walks can suit older children and fit older travellers, but trails are uneven, muddy and steep in places at over 2,000 m. Tell your guide about anyone's limits and choose a shorter route. If walking is difficult, birding along the forest roads around Lava is a gentler option.

faqs.q: How many days should I plan for Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Plan two nights in Lava for one full day in the park, with a spare morning in case of bad weather or permit problems. Serious birders may want three or four nights. Add a night in Rishop for the Kanchenjunga sunrise, which pairs well with a Neora Valley trip.

faqs.q: Can I trek deep into Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Longer treks into the interior, such as towards Rachela, are possible only with special permission from the forest department, porters, camping gear and an experienced guide. They are best arranged through specialist trekking operators well in advance. Day visitors stay on the shorter trails near the entry point.
